$comment: §49. Mission 1.70 offered this rule and did not add it. Change control requires it to be reviewed rather than carried forward silently or adopted because it is useful.

candidate.name: COVERAGE_SEMANTICS_MUST_DISTINGUISH_ATTEMPT_FROM_SUCCESS
candidate.why_1_70_declined: one shape seen on two routes is one instance. The standard Mission 1.67 set for itself is a second instance in a DIFFERENT shape.

the_question_asked_here: is the failure mode now demonstrated in a second genuinely different shape?

instances_considered.instance: Common Crawl and HTTP Archive, Mission 1.70
instances_considered.shape: an external publisher's coverage surface that does not state whether an attempted-and-failed item appears
instances_considered.note: the two routes together are ONE instance of this shape, which is what Mission 1.70 concluded

instances_considered.instance: the SROS bounded HTTP apparatus designed in this mission
instances_considered.shape: an apparatus we designed to avoid the failure
instances_considered.why_it_does_not_count: §49 states it directly and it is the right rule: designing AROUND a failure mode is not observing a second occurrence of it. If it counted, every registry rule could be promoted by writing a contract that respects it, and the registry would record our own intentions rather than what apparatuses actually do.

those failed on which targets were ELIGIBLE or on the temporal object, which the registry already covers under SAMPLING_IS_LOAD_BEARING, THE_RETRIEVABLE_FRAME_IS_NOT_THE_MEASURED_FRAME and THE_TEMPORAL_OBJECT_TEST. Attempt-versus-success is a different question and it was not what refused them.

why_usefulness_is_not_the_standard: the rule is genuinely useful and this mission's whole missingness contract is built on it. Adding it on that basis would make the registry a list of good ideas rather than a record of failure modes observed twice, which is the property that lets a later mission trust an entry without re-deriving it.
